title: Week 6 — Economic Dashboards and Data Storytelling
text:
Week 6 — Economic Dashboards and Data Storytelling
Week 4 prepared the data.
Week 5 generated evidence.
Week 6 asks students to communicate the evidence clearly.
The central question is:
How can we turn analysis into a dashboard that supports understanding and decision-making?
This week is not about making graphs look decorative. It is about designing an analytical communication product.



1. Learning Outcomes
By the end of this week, students should be able to:

explain the purpose of an economic dashboard
select charts based on analytical questions
build interactive Plotly graphs
combine indicators into a coherent dashboard
use titles, labels, hover information, and layout to support interpretation
avoid common dashboard design mistakes
write a short data story that connects evidence to economic meaning




2. Two-Hour Learning Plan








Time
Section
Main Focus




0-10 minutes
Week 5 recap
Main findings from exploratory analysis


10-25 minutes
Dashboard purpose
Decision support, not decoration


25-45 minutes
Chart selection
Match chart type to question


45-70 minutes
Interactive graphs
Plotly line, bar, and scatter charts


70-95 minutes
Dashboard layout
Build a multi-panel monitoring dashboard


95-115 minutes
Data storytelling
Claim, evidence, implication, caution


115-120 minutes
Assignment briefing
Final dashboard submission






3. Week 6 Learning Materials



Material
Purpose
Link




Week 6 Live Notebook
Build the dashboard in Google Colab
Open Week 6 Live Notebook


Macroeconomic Dataset
Download the CSV file used in class
Download sri_lanka_macro.csv


Plotly Guide
Reference for interactive charts
Open Plotly Python Guide



Inside Google Colab:
File -> Save a copy in Drive
Rename your copy:
Week06_IndexNumber_Name.ipynb



4. Why Week 6 Is the Next Step
Students have already learned how to:

run Python code
inspect and clean data
create variables
generate statistics
create graphs
interpret evidence

Week 6 combines those skills into one communication workflow.



Stage
Student Output




Week 4
Clean dataset


Week 5
Evidence and interpretation


Week 6
Dashboard and data story






5. What Is a Dashboard?
A dashboard is a structured visual interface that helps users understand important information quickly.
In economics, dashboards may be used to monitor:

inflation
GDP growth
exchange rates
reserves
unemployment
fiscal indicators
household welfare

A dashboard is not:
many charts placed on one page
A dashboard is:
a guided analytical view of a problem



6. Dashboard Design Questions
Before building a dashboard, answer:

Who is the audience?
What question should the dashboard answer?
Which indicators are most important?
Which charts best communicate those indicators?
What should the user notice first?
What interpretation should accompany the visuals?

For this course, the Week 6 dashboard answers:
How did Sri Lanka's macroeconomic conditions change across the period?



7. Chart Selection







Question
Recommended Chart




How did a variable change over time?
Line chart


Which year had the worst outcome?
Bar chart


Do two variables move together?
Scatter plot


Which indicators reached warning levels?
Table or highlighted indicators



The chart should follow the question.
Do not choose a graph only because it looks attractive.



8. Load the Data
import pandas as pd
import plotly.express as px
from plotly.subplots import make_subplots
import plotly.graph_objects as go

url = "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/kanishkawerawella/ECN4199_Website/main/data/sri_lanka_macro.csv"
data = pd.read_csv(url)

data["Exchange_Rate_Change"] = data["Exchange_Rate"].pct_change() * 100
data["Recession"] = data["GDP_Growth"] < 0



9. Interactive Line Chart
fig = px.line(
    data,
    x="Year",
    y="Inflation",
    markers=True,
    title="Inflation Over Time"
)

fig.show()
Use line charts for trends.
Interpretation:
The chart helps identify when inflation began to accelerate and when it returned toward lower levels.



10. Interactive Bar Chart
fig = px.bar(
    data,
    x="Year",
    y="GDP_Growth",
    color="GDP_Growth",
    title="GDP Growth by Year"
)

fig.show()
Use bar charts for comparisons.
Add interpretation:

Which year had the largest contraction?
Did the contraction coincide with high inflation?
What does this suggest about macroeconomic stress?




11. Interactive Scatter Plot
fig = px.scatter(
    data,
    x="Inflation",
    y="Exchange_Rate_Change",
    hover_name="Year",
    title="Inflation and Exchange Rate Change"
)

fig.show()
Use scatter plots for relationships.
Interpret carefully:
The chart can show association, but not causation.



12. Building a Monitoring Dashboard
A simple dashboard can combine multiple indicators.
fig = make_subplots(
    rows=3,
    cols=1,
    subplot_titles=(
        "Inflation",
        "GDP Growth",
        "Exchange Rate"
    )
)

fig.add_trace(
    go.Scatter(x=data["Year"], y=data["Inflation"], mode="lines+markers", name="Inflation"),
    row=1,
    col=1
)

fig.add_trace(
    go.Bar(x=data["Year"], y=data["GDP_Growth"], name="GDP Growth"),
    row=2,
    col=1
)

fig.add_trace(
    go.Scatter(x=data["Year"], y=data["Exchange_Rate"], mode="lines+markers", name="Exchange Rate"),
    row=3,
    col=1
)

fig.update_layout(
    height=850,
    title_text="Macroeconomic Monitoring Dashboard"
)

fig.show()



13. Dashboard Design Principles
Good dashboards are:

focused
readable
consistent
clearly labelled
connected to an analytical question
supported by interpretation

Avoid:

too many charts
unclear titles
missing units
random colors
decorative graphs without purpose
conclusions that go beyond the evidence




14. Data Storytelling
A dashboard should be accompanied by a short story.
Use this structure:



Part
Purpose




Claim
State the main pattern


Evidence
Refer to values or charts


Meaning
Explain why it matters economically


Caution
State what the dashboard cannot prove



Example:
The dashboard suggests that 2022 was the most severe macroeconomic stress point in the period. Inflation reached its highest value while GDP growth was strongly negative and the exchange rate increased sharply. This combination signals pressure on prices, output, and external stability. However, the dashboard is descriptive and should not be treated as a causal model.



15. Week 6 Output
By the end of Week 6, students should have:

at least three interactive charts
one multi-panel dashboard
clear titles, labels, and hover information
a short dashboard interpretation
one limitation or caution statement




16. Summary
Week 6 completes the applied analytics block.
The core lesson is:
Economic analysis becomes valuable when it is communicated clearly, honestly, and usefully.
Students should now be able to move from raw data to preparation, exploration, interpretation, and communication.

title: Week 4 — Preparing Economic Data for Analysis

Weeks 1-3 gave students the foundation:

running Python code
understanding variables and data types
importing and inspecting data

Week 4 is where those skills become a real analytical workflow.

This is one of the most important skills in industrial data analytics. A model, graph, dashboard, or AI-generated result is only as reliable as the data behind it.

title: Week 2 — Working with Data in Python
text:
In Week 1, we learned how to use Python as a calculator and how to execute simple commands.
This week, we begin working with the most important asset in modern economics:
DATA
Every day economists use data to answer questions such as:

Why are some people unemployed?
What determines wages?
Why does inflation increase?
Which districts experience higher poverty?
How does education affect earnings?
How does technology influence productivity?

Regardless of whether you become:

an economist
policy analyst
researcher
consultant
banker
data analyst

your ability to work with data will become increasingly important.
For this reason, Week 2 focuses on understanding how Python stores and organizes data.
Everything we do later in the course:

data visualization
dashboards
forecasting
machine learning
artificial intelligence

depends on concepts introduced this week.

title: Week 5 — Exploratory Economic Analysis
text:
Week 5 — Exploratory Economic Analysis
Week 4 focused on preparing data.
Week 5 focuses on using that prepared data to answer economic questions.
The central question is:
What does the evidence suggest?
This week is not mainly about producing graphs. It is about using statistics and visualizations to develop an economic interpretation.



1. Learning Outcomes
By the end of this week, students should be able to:

move from cleaned data to exploratory analysis
generate descriptive statistics for economic variables
compare averages, medians, minimums, maximums, and variation
interpret distributions and outliers
create graphs that match analytical questions
examine relationships between variables
distinguish correlation from causation
write a short evidence-based economic interpretation




2. Two-Hour Learning Plan








Time
Section
Main Focus




0-10 minutes
Week 4 recap
What makes data analysis-ready?


10-30 minutes
Analytical questions
Turning data into economic questions


30-50 minutes
Descriptive statistics
Level, spread, extremes


50-75 minutes
Distributions
Histograms and outliers


75-100 minutes
Trends and comparisons
Line and bar charts


100-115 minutes
Relationships
Scatter plots and correlation


115-120 minutes
Assignment briefing
Evidence note for Week 6 dashboard






3. Week 5 Learning Materials



Material
Purpose
Link




Week 5 Live Notebook
Complete exploratory analysis in Google Colab
Open Week 5 Live Notebook


Macroeconomic Dataset
Download the CSV file used in class
Download sri_lanka_macro.csv



Inside Google Colab:
File -> Save a copy in Drive
Rename your copy:
Week05_IndexNumber_Name.ipynb



4. Why Week 5 Is Not a Repeat of Week 4
Week 4 asked:
Is the data ready?
Week 5 asks:
What does the data say?
The same dataset is used, but the purpose changes.



Week
Main Task
Output




Week 4
Prepare data
Clean dataset and data-quality note


Week 5
Analyze data
Evidence, graphs, interpretation


Week 6
Communicate analysis
Interactive dashboard and story






5. Start With Analytical Questions
Exploratory analysis should be guided by questions.
Examples:

When did macroeconomic instability become most visible?
Which indicator shows the largest shock?
Did high inflation occur together with negative growth?
Did exchange rate movements coincide with inflation?
Which year appears most unusual?

Good analysis does not begin with a graph type.
It begins with a question.



6. Load and Prepare the Dataset
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

url = "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/kanishkawerawella/ECN4199_Website/main/data/sri_lanka_macro.csv"
data = pd.read_csv(url)

data["Exchange_Rate_Change"] = data["Exchange_Rate"].pct_change() * 100
data["Recession"] = data["GDP_Growth"] < 0
Check the data before analysis:
data.head()
data.info()
data.describe()



7. Descriptive Statistics
Descriptive statistics summarize the dataset.
data[["Inflation", "GDP_Growth", "Exchange_Rate_Change", "Reserves", "Unemployment"]].describe()
Interpretation should go beyond reading numbers.
Ask:

Which variable has the largest variation?
Which variable has the most extreme value?
Does the average hide important changes over time?
Which statistic best supports your interpretation?




8. Mean, Median, and Extreme Values
The mean is useful, but it can be distorted by extreme observations.
data["Inflation"].mean()
data["Inflation"].median()
data["Inflation"].max()
Interpretation:
If the mean is much higher than the median, extreme inflation years may be pulling the average upward.
This is especially important in crisis analysis.



9. Distributions
A distribution shows how values are spread.
plt.hist(data["Inflation"], bins=6)
plt.title("Distribution of Inflation")
plt.xlabel("Inflation Rate")
plt.ylabel("Number of Years")
plt.show()
Ask:

Are most values low, moderate, or high?
Are there extreme observations?
Does the distribution show stability or instability?




10. Trends Over Time
Line graphs are useful for time-series questions.
plt.plot(data["Year"], data["Inflation"], marker="o")
plt.title("Inflation Over Time")
plt.xlabel("Year")
plt.ylabel("Inflation Rate")
plt.show()
Interpretation should identify:

direction of change
turning points
crisis periods
recovery periods

Do not write:
The graph shows inflation.
Write:
Inflation remained relatively low before rising sharply in 2022, indicating a major macroeconomic shock.



11. Comparisons
Bar charts are useful when comparing discrete periods or categories.
plt.bar(data["Year"], data["GDP_Growth"])
plt.title("GDP Growth by Year")
plt.xlabel("Year")
plt.ylabel("GDP Growth")
plt.axhline(0, color="black", linewidth=1)
plt.show()
The zero line matters because it separates expansion from contraction.
Ask:

Which years show recession?
Was the decline mild or severe?
Does the recession coincide with other instability indicators?




12. Relationships Between Variables
Scatter plots are useful for studying relationships.
plt.scatter(data["Inflation"], data["Exchange_Rate_Change"])
plt.title("Inflation and Exchange Rate Change")
plt.xlabel("Inflation")
plt.ylabel("Exchange Rate Change")
plt.show()
Then calculate correlation:
data["Inflation"].corr(data["Exchange_Rate_Change"])
Important:
Correlation does not prove causation.
A good interpretation is cautious:
The variables appear to move together during crisis years, but this does not prove that one directly caused the other.



13. Evidence Table
Before writing the final interpretation, create a compact evidence table.
evidence = data[[
    "Year",
    "Inflation",
    "GDP_Growth",
    "Exchange_Rate_Change",
    "Reserves"
]]

evidence
Use the table to connect claims with values.
Weak claim:
The economy was unstable.
Stronger claim:
The economy shows strong instability in 2022, when inflation reached 46.4 percent and GDP growth was -7.8 percent.



14. Writing an Economic Interpretation
A useful interpretation has four parts:



Part
Question




Claim
What pattern did you find?


Evidence
Which value, graph, or statistic supports it?


Economic meaning
Why does it matter?


Caution
What can the analysis not prove?



Example:
The data suggest a severe macroeconomic shock in 2022. Inflation reached its highest value while GDP growth was strongly negative. This combination indicates pressure on household purchasing power and overall economic activity. However, the analysis is descriptive and does not prove the exact causal mechanism behind the crisis.



15. Week 5 Output
By the end of Week 5, students should have:

descriptive statistics
at least three graphs
one correlation result
an evidence table
a short economic interpretation
clear findings that can be used in the Week 6 dashboard




16. Summary
Week 5 turns prepared data into evidence.
The core lesson is:
Graphs and statistics are useful only when they support economic interpretation.
In Week 6, students will convert these findings into an interactive dashboard for communication and decision support.
